questions.q: In which year did India sign the Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with the Russian Federation, replacing the 1971 Indo-Soviet Treaty?
questions.a: 1993. A wrong answer (e.g., 1991 or 1995) reveals confusion between the Soviet collapse (Dec 1991) and the formalization of the new bilateral framework; students often miss the 14-month gap during which India operated without a treaty umbrella while negotiating terms that preserved defense supplies but dropped the ideological "socialist orientation" clause.

questions.q: Why did India continue to rely on Russian defense equipment after 1991 despite the availability of Western alternatives?
questions.a: Three interlocking reasons: (1) Compatibility — Indian armed forces were trained on Soviet/Russian platforms; switching would cost billions and decades. (2) Technology transfer — Russia offered licensed production (e.g., Su-30MKI, T-90 tanks) and cryogenic engine tech that the West denied. (3) Strategic trust — Russia supported India on Kashmir at the UN and did not impose sanctions after 1998 nuclear tests. A wrong answer focusing only on "cost" or "habit" misses the geopolitical calculation of maintaining a non-Western strategic lifeline.

questions.q: How did the simultaneous occurrence of the 1991 Balance of Payments crisis and the Soviet disintegration influence India's "Look East" policy?
questions.a: The dual crisis forced India to seek new markets, capital, and technology. With the Soviet bloc gone as a trading partner (rupee-rouble trade collapsed) and the West imposing conditionalities, India turned to Southeast Asia — ASEAN — for trade diversification and investment. The "Look East" policy (launched 1992) was thus a direct economic survival strategy triggered by the loss of the Soviet market and the IMF-led reform package. A wrong answer treating "Look East" as merely cultural or security-driven ignores the immediate economic compulsion.

questions.q: Compare India's engagement with Central Asian republics (1992-1995) with its engagement with Russia in the same period. What does the difference reveal about Indian strategic priorities?
questions.a: With Russia: high-level summits, defense treaties, nuclear cooperation — a "special and privileged strategic partnership" from day one. With Central Asia: limited to cultural exchanges, technical aid, and rhetorical support for sovereignty — no defense pacts, minimal trade. The asymmetry reveals India prioritized securing the strategic core (Russia as great power, UN veto holder, defense supplier) over the peripheral republics, which lacked hard power and were geographically separated by Afghanistan/Pakistan. A wrong answer claiming "equal engagement" ignores the resource constraints and hierarchy in Indian foreign policy.

questions.q: Critique the argument: "India's post-1991 foreign policy abandoned non-alignment and became pro-American."
questions.a: The argument is flawed. Evidence against: (1) India refused to join US-led alliances or sign foundational military agreements (COMCASA, BECA) until 2018-2020. (2) India maintained and deepened defense ties with Russia (S-400 deal despite US CAATSA threat). (3) India championed multipolarity (RIC, BRICS, SCO) explicitly to counter unipolarity. (4) India's 1998 nuclear tests defied US pressure. What changed: non-alignment evolved into "multi-alignment" — engaging all major powers simultaneously without surrendering autonomy. A wrong answer equating "engagement with US" with "abandonment of non-alignment" fails to distinguish tactical alignment from strategic subordination.

questions.q: Draft a 50-word diplomatic communiqué that India might have issued in January 1992 recognizing the Russian Federation as the successor state to the USSR, incorporating the principles of continuity, sovereign equality, and multipolarity.
questions.a: Sample: "India recognizes the Russian Federation as the continuator state of the USSR, inheriting its UN Security Council seat and treaty obligations. We reaffirm our commitment to the 1971 Treaty's spirit of peace, friendship, and cooperation, adapted to new realities. India stands for a multipolar world based on sovereign equality and non-interference." A poor answer omits "continuator state" (legal term), misses the UNSC seat reference, or uses Cold War rhetoric ("socialist solidarity") instead of sovereign equality.
